naming-konecta-brand-story.title: Why We Named the Brand Konecta: Comparing the Candidates
naming-konecta-brand-story.summary: How we landed on Konecta after starting with the working name Noriter Beauty Center — the criteria we used to compare candidates and the meaning built into the name.
naming-konecta-brand-story.content:
Before I settled on the name Konecta, I already had another name — one I'd even set up an Instagram account for: Noriter Beauty Center, with the handle @noriter_beautycenter. But I never actually launched the business under that name.

The reason was simple. When I said the word “Noriter” to a Spanish or English speaker for the first time, it sounded unfamiliar and didn't convey any meaning at all. If a brand name can't explain what the business actually does, you've already lost half the battle before you even get to make your pitch.

In the end, the name is the first sentence that shows what kind of bridge this brand is building.

So I went back through the candidate names and narrowed my criteria to three. First, is it easy to pronounce for both Spanish and English speakers? Second, are the Instagram handle and domain actually available to use? Third, does the name itself explain what the business does — connecting Korean cosmetics with the Latin American market? Surprisingly few names satisfied all three at once.

After comparing several candidates, the name I landed on was Konecta — a blend of “Korea” and the Spanish word conecta (“connects”). It's easy to pronounce in both language worlds, and best of all, the meaning of “connection” is built right into the name itself.

Starting from the fact that each of the Andes' different climates comes with different skin concerns, and connecting Latin American consumers with products that actually match their real concerns — instead of just bringing over whatever sells well in Korea — that's the core of what Konecta is trying to do. That's ultimately why I spent so long agonizing over a single name: I believed the name itself had to show what kind of bridge this brand would build.

peru-startup-look-beyond-latin-america.title: Planning to enter the Latin American market? Don't just look at Peru — look at the whole continent
peru-startup-look-beyond-latin-america.summary: Why, when you're building a one-person import business out of Peru, Lima should be your gateway to sizing up the whole South American market — not the end point.
peru-startup-look-beyond-latin-america.content:
Are you preparing to enter Latin America with only the Peruvian market in mind? There's something that people taking their first steps into Peru as solo traders often miss. Peru is definitely a good starting point, but seen against the whole of Latin America, it's just one market among many.

Lima is both the capital of Peru and a city that solo traders preparing to enter Latin America pass through often. That's because it has good logistics access with a port and airport close together, and it also acts as a gateway to other South American countries. So starting your business in Peru naturally gives you the chance to get a feel for the flow of the whole Latin American market at the same time.

In the end, the key to starting a business in Peru is not stopping at Peru alone.

Even within Latin America, consumer tendencies and distribution structures differ from country to country. That means an approach proven in Peru might not work the same way in Chile or Colombia. So rather than preparing several countries at once from the very start, I'd recommend first confirming the response with small-batch trades in Peru, then expanding one by one into other Latin American markets.

Looking at real cases of solo traders who started in Lima and expanded across Latin America, none of them stayed locked into just one country from the beginning. They carried forward the startup experience they built in Peru along with research on neighboring markets, and put that experience to direct use when moving into the next market.

In the end, the key to starting a business in Peru is not stopping at Peru alone. I believe that using Lima as a gateway and picturing all of Latin America on a wider map is the safest approach for anyone jumping into their first market as a solo trader.

solo-trade-latin-america-small-batch.title: Entering the Latin American market as a solo trader: start small
solo-trade-latin-america-small-batch.summary: How to lower your risk by starting with small-batch orders — and how to line up sourcing, customs, and forwarders — when you're taking on markets like Peru or Chile solo.
solo-trade-latin-america-small-batch.content:
If you want to take on a market like Peru or Chile, where Korean cosmetics aren't yet well known, I'd recommend starting with small-batch trades as a solo trader rather than putting in a lot of capital from day one. Solo trading is a way of doing business where an individual can deal directly with overseas buyers without a separate corporation or a large organization, and lately more and more people are using it to take on emerging markets like Latin America.

The most common mistake people make when starting out in trade is setting the order volume too high from the beginning. In a market like Latin America, where consumer response is hard to predict, it's safer to first confirm the response with small-batch trades and then gradually increase the volume. The biggest advantage of small-batch trading is that even if you make a mistake, you still have room to recover.

The biggest advantage of small-batch trading is that even if you make a mistake, you still have room to recover.

The practical work you need to prepare in the early stages of a startup can be broken down into three main areas: sourcing, customs, and forwarders. Sourcing is the process of deciding which products to supply and under what terms; customs refers to the documents and procedures needed to clear the local customs authority in Latin America; and a forwarder is the company that actually transports the cargo. Since sanitary registration and customs standards differ from country to country in Latin America, it's safer to check them in advance for each country you plan to enter.

Peru and Chile also differ in consumer tendencies and distribution structure, so it's hard to apply experience from one country directly to the other. You also need to account for the possibility that shipping times may run longer than expected — and the surest way to get a feel for these variables is to run into them directly through small-batch trades.

To sum up, the key to entering the Latin American market as a solo trader is lowering your risk with small-batch trades while learning the sourcing, customs, and forwarder processes one at a time. Rather than waiting until you're perfectly prepared to start, starting small and building up experience is the safer approach in a market with as many variables as Latin America.

brand-name-konecta-story.title: One Name, One First Promise: The Story Behind the Brand Konecta
brand-name-konecta-story.summary: How we landed on the name Konecta, carrying a promise to connect Korean cosmetics with Latin American consumers — a plain, honest look at how we got there.
brand-name-konecta-story.content:
When we were starting the brand, the thing we agonized over the longest wasn't actually the product — it was the name. As we prepared to introduce Korean cosmetics to consumers in Peru and Chile, we realized we needed a name that would feel natural to people in both countries. There was also something we'd come to understand from years of working in skincare and semi-permanent makeup: the first thing that ever reaches a consumer isn't the product, it's the name.

So we wrote down a list of candidate names and spent time reading each one aloud. We had everything from names with a Korean feel, to names with local flavor, to names that emphasized the product itself. But once we actually said them out loud, the shortcomings started to show one by one. Some names were easy to say in Korean but unfamiliar to Spanish speakers; others felt natural locally but sounded awkward to Korean consumers. We weren't trying to build some grand naming story — it was really just a plain, honest process of comparing candidates and reconfirming what our brand was actually trying to do.

For a brand built around linking Korean cosmetics with South American consumers, no meaning could have fit better.

The name that survived that process was Konecta. It comes from the Spanish verb conectar — "to connect." For a brand built around linking Korean cosmetics with South American consumers, no meaning could have fit better. The pronunciation was decisive too: it reads naturally for both Korean and Spanish speakers. In the end, what set Konecta apart from the other candidates was that it satisfied both meaning and sound at once.

Something changed once we settled on the name. We felt a responsibility to actually live up to the idea of "connection," not just keep it in the name. That's also why, instead of simply bringing Korean products over as-is, we try to find the points where they genuinely meet local skin and preferences. It's the same reason we explain the meaning behind the name Konecta every time we introduce the brand — because a single name naturally conveys our goal of being a small bridge between Korea and Peru, and between Korea and Chile.

We think of the meaning behind the name Konecta as a promise we need to keep going forward. It wasn't chosen with some grand plan — it was a plain, honest choice — but the direction it points to, connection, is clear. Next time, we'll come back with a more concrete story of how that name is actually taking shape.

chile-trade-no-capital-small-lot.title: Can You Start Trading With Chile on No Capital? A Startup Approach Built on Small-Batch Deals
chile-trade-no-capital-small-lot.summary: For anyone hoping to start trading with Chile without a lot of capital behind them, here's a rundown of how to build a near-no-capital startup around small-batch deals.
chile-trade-no-capital-small-lot.content:
When you decide to start trading, the first thing that gets in the way is capital. If you think you need to sign contracts for large volumes, secure a warehouse, and set aside a large lump sum before you can even begin, the whole idea starts to feel overwhelming. But in a market like Chile, where domestic companies haven't entered in force yet, taking your first step through small-batch deals — rather than chasing bulk trade from day one — turns out to be the more realistic approach. Let's start by clarifying exactly what "starting a business with no capital" actually means.

The key to building a trading business in Chile isn't lining up a large amount of capital first — it's confirming the market and building trust through small-batch trading first.

Starting with no capital doesn't literally mean spending no money at all — it means opening up trade with minimal inventory and small order volumes, without a large upfront investment. Instead of a large warehouse or bulk purchase contracts, think of it as an approach where you exchange only what you need in small amounts, spreading the risk out into smaller pieces you can manage. Taking the small-batch route also removes a good deal of the burden that comes with stockpiling inventory early on and then having sales slow down.

Small-batch trading has a different feel from the negotiation stage onward, too. Rather than asking a new buyer for a large order right away, proposing a small sample-level order is a much more natural way to start the relationship. Buyers, for their part, often want to confirm quality or market response first, so proposing to start small can itself be the first step toward building trust. Being able to handle variables like shipping costs or exchange-rate swings in smaller pieces, instead of all at once, is another real advantage of small-batch trading.

There are a few things in the preparation process that are easy to overlook. Customs and paperwork can vary depending on the product and timing, so it's safer to confirm the exact tariff rates and regulations in advance through a customs broker or the relevant authority. On top of that, verifying the trustworthiness of your trading partner, and clearly agreeing on payment terms — whether it's upfront or deferred — needs careful attention even at the small-batch stage. Since Chile is a Spanish-speaking market, it's also worth factoring in some time to understand the local communication style and distribution structure.

In the end, the most stable path is to start small in the early stages — with minimal inventory and something close to no capital — and expand volume and product range as trust builds through continued trading. The key to building a trading business in Chile isn't lining up a large amount of capital first; it's confirming the market and building trust through small-batch trading first. If you're just starting to prepare for the Chilean market, we'd recommend reviewing the small-batch approach we covered today, one step at a time.

peru-chile-buyer-lima-trade-office.title: The First Step Into South America: Where to Find Buyers in Peru and Chile
peru-chile-buyer-lima-trade-office.summary: A rundown of how to use KOTRA's Lima trade office and industry resources to find buyers in Peru and Chile.
peru-chile-buyer-lima-trade-office.content:
If you're looking to introduce cosmetics into the South American market, the first thing you'll likely get stuck on is where to even begin looking for buyers in Peru or Chile. I ran into the same question while preparing to expand into South America, so I wanted to put together some of the practical information I found useful along the way.

The first place I checked was KOTRA. KOTRA runs a trade office in Lima, Peru, which helps connect local companies with export opportunities and buyers. Its website, Export24, actually lists a program called Prospective Buyer Discovery Support, so if you're just starting to look into the Peruvian market, you can reach out through that channel to ask about buyer information. KOTRA also operates trade offices across several other South American countries, including Chile, so it turned out to be more efficient in practice to look up the contact office for each country separately.

Beyond trade offices, industry resources are worth checking too. The Korea Cosmetic Association's website has published interviews with buyers who've entered the Chilean market, covering how K-beauty has been gaining traction there. The Korea Trade Insurance Corporation has also released cosmetics buyer information through the public data portal at times — useful as a reference for getting a sense of the market before reaching out to Peruvian or Chilean buyers directly.

In the end, buyer discovery comes down to how accurately you've prepared your information.

I've heard more than once that, practically speaking, it's a good idea to prepare a company profile and product information before requesting a buyer consultation. Buyers in Peru and Chile reportedly check product certification documents and ingredient information quite closely, so having your minimum order quantity and pricing policy ready in advance makes the first conversation go much more smoothly. Given variables like language and time zones, it also helps to let buyers know in advance what hours you're available to respond.

It's also worth knowing that, for a first move into South America, it's common to start with small sample trades rather than large contracts. And since Peru and Chile have different market characteristics, the research also confirmed that it's better to prepare for the two countries separately rather than taking the same approach to both.

In the end, buyer discovery comes down to how accurately you've prepared your information. Securing local information first through a credible institution like KOTRA, then working through the Peruvian and Chilean markets one at a time starting from the Lima trade office, feels like the realistic first step into South America.

I hope this is a small help to anyone preparing for the Peruvian or Chilean market.

dongdaemun-first-sourcing-day.title: At Dawn in Dongdaemun: The Day I Learned Cosmetics Sourcing Firsthand
dongdaemun-first-sourcing-day.summary: A record of the day I first saw and picked out cosmetics in person at a domestic wholesale market, and what I learned in the process.
dongdaemun-first-sourcing-day.content:
There's a clear limit to choosing cosmetics based only on photos on a screen. There's more than you'd think that you can only really know by touching a product — things like color payoff, texture, and how clean the packaging finish is. On a recent trip to a domestic wholesale market for my first sourcing run, I felt that difference firsthand.

I'd heard that a lot of stores open before dawn, so I headed out early. What greeted me when I arrived was far busier than I expected. Plenty of people were already moving between stores, each with their own purpose, and just finding the section I was looking for in the middle of it all wasn't easy.

Because I hadn't mapped out a route beforehand, I ended up circling the same alley several times. Even after finally finding the area where the cosmetics stores were clustered, things didn't get much easier. There were moments where I hesitated, unsure how to ask about prices or where to even start the conversation. It felt like a natural part of doing this for the first time, but it also left me determined to plan my route ahead of time next time.

In the end, it was a day that taught me that seeing, touching, and checking things in person is truly the most reliable way to choose cosmetics.

It wasn't all trial and error, though. Once I actually dabbed products on the back of my hand and smelled them, details I could never have picked up from photos alone started coming through. It reconfirmed something important: the more a cosmetic's key qualities — texture, how it spreads on skin — matter, the harder they are to judge from a screen. Being able to closely examine details like packaging finish and container material was also something only possible by being there in person.

Getting samples on the spot and comparing several products side by side in small amounts was another thing that set this apart from sourcing online. By keeping only the products whose color and texture I'd confirmed myself as candidates, my own criteria for choosing cosmetics became noticeably clearer than before.

I'm also involved in introducing cosmetics sourced domestically into South American markets like Peru and Chile. Maybe that's why this experience really drove home how much the criteria you use to choose products at this early stage shapes the whole direction that follows.

It wasn't a perfectly smooth day. But I want to keep even the trial and error as part of the record. In the end, it was a day that taught me that seeing, touching, and checking things in person is truly the most reliable way to choose cosmetics.

I'll share the next sourcing story soon.

customs-forwarder-cost-no-capital.title: Get a Few Forwarder Quotes, and Customs Costs Start to Come Into Focus
customs-forwarder-cost-no-capital.summary: A look at how to estimate customs and forwarder costs when preparing to trade and export with little to no capital.
customs-forwarder-cost-no-capital.content:
When you're first preparing to trade or export, the biggest worry that comes up is cost. Customs and forwarder fees in particular can feel especially confusing, since even the terminology is unfamiliar — it's hard to know where to even begin calculating. Fortunately, getting a handle on these costs doesn't require deep pockets. Even with no capital, requesting just a few quotes is enough to get a rough sense of the scale involved.

Let's start with the terms. A forwarder is a logistics company that handles freight shipping, paperwork, and customs procedures on your behalf. For a solo trader preparing an export on their own, a forwarder essentially acts as your logistics team. Customs refers to the process by which goods are officially cleared in and out as they cross a country's border, verified by that country's customs authority. Since handling this process yourself is complicated, it's typically done through a forwarder.

In the end, the key to managing trade and export costs is comparing forwarder quotes across several companies and learning the customs process firsthand through small-batch trading.

Your first point of contact with a forwarder isn't a contract — it's a quote request. Quote consultations are usually free, so you can compare several companies side by side even without any capital. If you're trading in small volumes, there's also the option of using international courier services instead of a container, which can save on warehousing fees and part of the customs handling fee — a route often chosen by people just starting out in trade and export. Quotes can vary quite a bit between companies depending on cargo type, weight, and destination, so we'd recommend getting quotes from at least two or three forwarders and carefully checking whether customs costs are included in the total.

There are a few things worth having ready if you want to estimate customs costs before exporting. First, you'll need your product's HS code to know the exact tariff rate — since rates vary by product and country, the most accurate way to confirm this is directly through the destination country's customs authority or your forwarder before you actually export. It's also a good idea to prepare the documents customs requires, like invoices and packing lists, well in advance. The smaller your shipment, the larger the customs handling fee tends to feel relative to the cargo itself, so it's also worth comparing handling fees specifically across different forwarders.

If you're preparing to trade and export with no capital, it's safer to start with small-batch trading rather than moving large volumes from the start. Once you've gotten a forwarder quote and been through the customs process firsthand, it becomes much easier to predict costs for your next export. Repeat the cycle of comparing quotes and trading in small batches a few times, and the cost structure of customs and forwarding naturally starts to come into focus — and the sense of being overwhelmed that you started with gradually fades.

In the end, the key to managing trade and export costs is comparing forwarder quotes across several companies and learning the customs process firsthand through small-batch trading. You don't need to have everything perfectly prepared from the start. The process of checking things off one by one is, in itself, already solid preparation.

peru-solo-trader-small-batch.title: Opening the Peruvian Market Through Small-Batch Trading: A Solo Trader's Choice
peru-solo-trader-small-batch.summary: For solo traders preparing to enter Peru on their own — how to confirm market response through small-batch trading first, then expand across South America.
peru-solo-trader-small-batch.content:
If you're a solo trader preparing to enter Peru on your own, you're probably wondering what the safest way to start is. The short answer: in an unfamiliar South American market like Peru, confirming the response through small-batch trading first is a far safer approach than trying to scale up volume right away.

Solo trading refers to a way of starting a business where one person handles the entire trade process — sourcing, customs, shipping, customer service — without a separate organization behind them. Because everything rests on one person, if you enter an unfamiliar market like Peru with a large volume and the response turns out different from what you expected, you end up carrying that burden entirely on your own. Small-batch trading reduces that risk while buying you time to learn the market.

Peru is often mentioned as one of the South American countries where interest in Korean products has stayed steady. That said, distribution structures and consumer response vary quite a bit from country to country across South America, so it's hard to assume that what works in Peru will translate directly to another South American country. That's why using Peru as a first foothold — testing the response repeatedly in small batches, then deciding on the next market based on that experience — becomes a realistic strategy for a solo trader. Since you don't need to secure large inventory upfront, small-batch trading also has the advantage of lowering both initial cost and inventory burden.

The key to a solo trader's Peru business is learning the market through small-batch trading rather than aiming for large volume from the start, then expanding that experience across South America.

There are a few things worth checking before diving into small-batch trading in earnest. It's worth understanding in advance what documents and procedures are needed to clear customs in Peru for whatever you're shipping. Since a solo trader handles this alone, the paperwork stage often takes longer than expected — getting familiar with the flow at the small-batch stage makes it easier later when you expand into other South American markets. Securing a channel to communicate with local partners or buyers in Peru is another important part of preparation, since with smaller shipments, the key is getting local feedback quickly and applying it to the next deal right away. Checking shipping lead times, cost structure, and payment methods at the small-batch stage also lets you plan much more concretely for when it's time to scale up volume.

A solo trader who learns the Peruvian market through small-batch trading can carry that experience into other South American countries as well. Which products got a good response, and which communication methods worked — the small-batch trading process itself in Peru becomes real, practical data on both. The details differ from country to country across South America, but the instincts built through small-batch trading in Peru still serve as a foundation in a new market.

In short, the key to a solo trader's Peru business is learning the market through small-batch trading rather than aiming for large volume from the start, then expanding that experience across South America. We hope this is helpful to solo traders taking their first step in Peru through small-batch trading.

no-capital-export-small-batch.title: No-Capital Export Startups: Solo Traders Who Start With Small-Batch Deals
no-capital-export-small-batch.summary: For solo traders without much capital behind them — the practical order of steps for starting an export business close to capital-free, using small-batch trading.
no-capital-export-small-batch.content:
There are moments when you hesitate over whether it's really okay to start an export business without much capital. The short answer: even in a near-no-capital situation, using small-batch trading makes starting an export business a genuinely viable option. The key isn't pushing for large volume from day one — it's starting small and confirming the response as you go.

The key isn't pushing for large volume from day one — it's starting small and confirming the response as you go.

Solo trading means a form of business where one person, without a separate organization, handles the entire process directly — sourcing, exporting, and settlement. Having no budget for additional staff also means that a near-no-capital approach can actually be a better fit for a solo trader. "No capital" here doesn't mean having no money at all — it's closer to meaning you're not using a capital-intensive approach of buying up large inventory in advance. With small-batch trading, you don't need to secure large volumes of product all at once; you can source just what you need, confirm the actual response, and then decide on the next round.

If you have no export experience, the paperwork and procedures alone can feel unfamiliar — and small-batch trading helps ease that burden too. Since you're not stockpiling large inventory, you avoid a situation where you'd have to shoulder the full burden alone if the response turns out different from what you expected. Small-batch trading is in fact often cited as a way to lower the initial capital burden, and it's particularly effective for gradually finding the products and methods that get a good response through several small attempts.

There are a few things worth settling before starting in earnest. You need to first decide which products to sell through which channels — without a clear direction, it's easy to waste time and money even at the small-batch stage. Rather than having everything perfectly in place from the start, it's more realistic to fill things in one at a time, at your own pace. Setting up a channel to communicate smoothly with your sourcing contacts, getting familiar with export documentation procedures in advance, and confirming payment methods and settlement cycles — sorting all of this out gradually at the small-batch stage makes the next stage much easier to move into. The less financial cushion you have, the more a single payment timing issue can affect your business's stability, so this is worth looking at especially carefully.

Once you've built up a feel for things through small-batch trading, you can gradually increase volume based on that experience. Because you didn't commit a lot of capital from the start, the burden isn't heavy even if results turn out differently than expected — that's a clear advantage of this approach. Moments where you have to make decisions, big and small, on your own will keep coming, but you can trust the instincts you've built at the small-batch stage to guide your judgment. The biggest value of this approach is that you get to learn the market yourself and grow the business at your own pace.

In short, starting an export business through small-batch trading is a genuinely realistic option even without sufficient capital. We hope this is helpful to anyone looking to take a safe first step without a lot of capital behind them.

peru-chile-beauty-market-overview.title: The Peru-Chile Beauty Market: The More We Learn, the More Questions We Have
peru-chile-beauty-market-overview.summary: While researching the Peru and Chile beauty markets to prepare K-beauty's move into South America, here's what we found — sticking only to facts we could actually confirm.
peru-chile-beauty-market-overview.content:
The first question we ran into while getting Konecta ready was simple: what even is the South American market? Just searching online turns up a flood of numbers — rankings, market shares, you name it — but when you actually try to trace where those numbers came from, the source is often shaky at best. So we decided we wouldn't use any figure we couldn't verify, and instead wanted to lay out today what we actually learned firsthand while researching.

Understanding regional skin types first, and curating products to match, is the order that makes sense — researching this only made that clearer to us.

The first assumption that fell apart was the idea that "South America is one market." Just looking at Peru, the capital Lima has a dry, desert-like coastal climate, but head a bit inland and you run into the intense UV of the Andean highlands. Chile spans everything from the northern desert to the cold climate of Patagonia in the south, all within one country. When the climate varies this much, skin concerns naturally vary too.

That made us realize it would be risky to bring a product over as-is just because "it sells well in Korea." In a dry coastal area, moisture and sun care should come first; in a high-altitude area, protecting the skin barrier should come first. Understanding regional skin types first, and curating products to match, is the order that makes sense — researching this only made that clearer to us.

As for numbers like market size or K-beauty's market share, we honestly haven't yet found a source we'd trust for this research, so we deliberately left them out of this post. What we could confirm, looking at social media and local communities, was more of a general sense: mentions of Korean skincare routines and ingredients come up consistently. Getting a feel for that kind of atmosphere first, rather than chasing exact figures, feels like the step we actually need right now.

We'll keep researching the market going forward, but we don't want to force in anything we haven't confirmed. Instead, we'll keep building up information with clear sources, one piece at a time, and only publish on this blog what we've verified ourselves. We'll share the next update soon.
